items.name: part1
items.direction: Narrate this as a popular geography YouTube channel's long-form explainer. The Narrator is a deep, warm, confident storyteller: curious and brisk but never rushed, with natural emphasis, building intrigue towards the reveal, a short comic pause before each punchline, and real awe at the big moments. Chars voices funny cartoon characters: short and punchy. Read numbers naturally.
lines: Narrator
Every night, the Moon just hangs there, quietly. But it isn't quiet at all. It's the wreckage of the most violent crash in Earth's history.
Narrator
And the planet that caused that crash? It never left. Parts of it may still be buried deep inside the Earth, right under your feet.
Narrator
So why do we even have a Moon? Let's start with how weird it is.
Narrator
Mercury has no moon. Venus has none either. Mars has two, but they're tiny lumps of rock, the biggest only about twenty-two kilometres across.
Narrator
And then there's us. Our Moon is more than a quarter as wide as the Earth itself. For a rocky planet, that's absurdly big.
Chars
[sassy, vain, theatrical diva] Absurdly big? I prefer... fabulous.
Narrator
For centuries, nobody could explain where it came from. Maybe the Earth captured a passing rock. Maybe the Moon spun off a fast-spinning Earth.
Narrator
Then, between 1969 and 1972, Apollo astronauts brought back three hundred and eighty-two kilograms of Moon rock. And the rocks told a very strange story.
Narrator
Chemically, Moon rock looks almost exactly like the rock in Earth's mantle. Same fingerprints. As if the Moon had been made from a piece of the Earth.
Narrator
But no simple theory could explain that. Until scientists imagined something far more violent.
Narrator
About four and a half billion years ago, the young Earth wasn't alone in its orbit. A second planet, about the size of Mars, was heading straight for it.
Narrator
Scientists call it THEE-uh, after the mother of the Moon goddess in Greek myth.
Chars
[innocent, cheerful, a little too sweet] I just wanted to say hello.

lines: Narrator
It hit the Earth at a glancing angle, at around ten kilometres per second. The crash melted both planets and blasted a huge cloud of molten rock and vapour into space.
Narrator
For a while, the Earth may have looked like a glowing ball of magma, wrapped in a ring of debris.
Narrator
Older models said the debris took months or years to clump into a Moon. But a 2022 supercomputer simulation found it could have happened in just a few hours.
Narrator
And that new Moon was close. Maybe more than ten times closer than today. In the sky, it would have looked enormous.
Narrator
A day on Earth back then may have lasted only about five or six hours.
Chars
[dizzy, exhausted, grumpy] Five-hour days? I got nothing done.
Narrator
So the Moon was born in a disaster. But here's the thing. That disaster may be the reason Earth became such a good home.
Narrator
First, the tides. The Moon's gravity pulls on our oceans, lifting them into two bulges that sweep around the planet every day.
Narrator
Those tides act like a brake. Over billions of years, they slowed Earth's spin from those crazy five-hour days to the twenty-four hours we have now.
Narrator
And as Earth slows down, the Moon drifts away. Apollo astronauts left mirrors on the Moon, and by bouncing lasers off them, we can measure it: about three point eight centimetres every year.
Narrator
That's roughly as fast as your fingernails grow.
Narrator
The Moon also helps keep Earth's tilt steady. That tilt gives us our seasons. Without a big Moon, it could swing around far more over millions of years, and climates could change wildly.

lines: Narrator
And there's a lucky coincidence. The Sun is about four hundred times wider than the Moon, but also about four hundred times farther away. So from Earth, they look almost the same size.
Narrator
That's why we get total solar eclipses. But it won't last. As the Moon drifts away, in about six hundred million years, total eclipses will stop forever.
Chars
[sassy, vain, theatrical diva] Enjoy me while you can.
Narrator
But remember that other planet? THEE-uh. Where did it go?
Narrator
Most of THEE-uh was swallowed by the Earth. And deep down, near the core, scientists have found two giant, mysterious blobs of rock. One under Africa, one under the Pacific.
Narrator
Each one is bigger than a continent, and denser than the rock around it. Earthquake waves slow down when they pass through them.
Narrator
In 2023, a team of scientists ran new simulations and suggested something wild. Those blobs could be the remains of THEE-uh itself, still sitting at the bottom of Earth's mantle.
Chars
[sweet but creepy, slow, whispering] Hello again. I never left.
Narrator
It's still being tested. But if it's right, the Moon isn't just a rock in the sky. It's the other half of a crime scene, and the evidence is inside our own planet.
Narrator

And India has been part of the investigation. Chandrayaan-1, launched in 2008, helped find signs of water on the Moon. And in 2023, Chandrayaan-3 became the first mission to land near the Moon's south pole.
Narrator
So next time you look at the Moon, remember. It's not just a light in the sky. It's what's left of the day the Earth was hit by another world.
Narrator
This is Bhoogol. Follow for more Geography Fun Facts.
